# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **Forty-four billion dollars in notes will fund SpaceX's Vera Rubin purchase.**

**What You Need to Know:** Apollo and Goldman Sachs have priced about forty-four billion dollars in notes to finance SpaceX's purchase of Nvidia Vera Rubin chips and related equipment. High-bandwidth memory is projected to take 23 percent of the three big suppliers' DRAM wafer starts in 2026 and nearly 30 percent in 2027. In Osaka, a 48-megawatt hall under a CyrusOne and KEP joint venture has topped out.

### Top Story
Apollo Global Management and Goldman Sachs priced about $44 billion in senior and subordinated notes to buy GPUs and related equipment for SpaceX, citybiz reported, after the book was oversubscribed and the financing was increased. The companies call it the largest GPU financing executed to date. The notes back SpaceX's terrestrial compute build with Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips. Funds and accounts managed by BlackRock and Goldman Sachs Asset Management, plus capital accounts advised by KKR, joined as anchor commitments. A BASENOR account of the same announcement says the hardware sits in Saturn Funding Trust, which leases it back to SpaceX so the debt stays off the corporate balance sheet, and that lenders required the GPUs — the collateral — to remain on Earth in U.S. data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX. Lease schedules start when the equipment is delivered in the first half of 2027. Apollo partner Jamshid Ehsani said SpaceX is "one of the most ambitious builders of compute in the world." Source: [citybiz.co](https://www.citybiz.co/article/937031/apollo-and-goldman-sachs-price-44-billion-spacex-gpu-financing-for-nvidia-vera-rubin-ai-infrastructure/) Source: [basenor.com](https://www.basenor.com/blogs/news/spacex-lands-record-44b-financing-to-buy-nvidia-vera-rubin-ai-chips)

### Silicon
**HBM Memory Shortage: 23% of DRAM Wafers, 30% by 2027: shattered.io**
TrendForce projects that high-bandwidth memory will take 23 percent of DRAM wafer input at Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron in 2026 and nearly 30 percent in 2027, shattered.io reported, because HBM needs three to four times as much wafer capacity as general-purpose DRAM. A shortage tracker summarized by Futu News puts HBM supply at roughly 58 percent of estimated first-quarter demand. TrendForce expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise 10 to 15 percent quarter over quarter in the fourth quarter, while NAND is falling. SK hynix says its HBM and related DRAM are sold out through 2029, and Micron reportedly covers only half to two-thirds of customer demand. SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won said the current shortage could continue until 2030, and SK hynix chief executive Kwak Noh-jung said customer demand will remain higher than supply capacity even beyond 2030. New capacity from China's CXMT clouds the 2028 outlook, and major new memory fabs are not expected to add meaningful output before around 2028. Source: [shattered.io](https://shattered.io/hbm-memory-shortage-23-percent-dram-wafers-nears-30-percent-2027-trendforce/)

**NVIDIA Vera CPU coming to CoreWeave with 3x faster agent sandboxes: CoreWeave**
Nvidia's Vera CPU is coming soon to CoreWeave, the company posted, and it is described there as the first CPU purpose-built for AI agents. Diana Aung, senior product manager at Nvidia, shared a measurement of more than 3x faster agent-sandbox startup than on an alternative x86 CPU. The figure is a startup-time comparison, not a claim that the CPU has shipped into CoreWeave's cloud. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/CoreWeave/status/2123899285032825320)

**World’s First Mass Production of Ultrahigh-Mobility Oxide Technology Paves the Way for a New Generation of Displays: Semiconductor Digest**
TCL CSOT has mass-produced ultrahigh-mobility oxide technology on an 8.6-generation line, Semiconductor Digest reported, and calls the run a world first. The stated electron mobility is about 50 square centimetres per volt per second. Source: [semiconductor-digest.com](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/worlds-first-mass-production-of-ultrahigh-mobility-oxide-technology-paves-the-way-for-a-new-generation-of-displays/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=worlds-first-mass-production-of-ultrahigh-mobility-oxide-technology-paves-the-way-for-a-new-generation-of-displays)

### Data Centres & Power
**CyrusOne and KEP top out 48MW data center in Osaka, Japan: Data Center Dynamics**
Under construction in Osaka, a 48-megawatt data center from CyrusOne and KEP has topped out, Data Center Dynamics reported. It is the first facility under the pair's Japanese joint venture. Topped out is not the same as energized. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/cyrusone-and-kep-top-out-48mw-data-center-in-osaka-japan/)

**Microsoft files for 316.7-acre data center campus in Mecklenburg County, Virginia: Data Center Dynamics**
Announced by filing, Microsoft is seeking a 316.7-acre data center campus in Mecklenburg County, Virginia, Data Center Dynamics reported. The plan is five data center buildings on the site. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/microsoft-files-for-3167-acre-data-center-campus-in-mecklenburg-county-virginia/)

**US Senate passes bill requiring data centers to pay more for grid infrastructure: Data Center Dynamics**
The U.S. Senate has passed a bill requiring data centers to pay more for grid infrastructure, Data Center Dynamics reported. The bill now heads to the House. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/us-senate-passes-bill-requiring-data-centers-to-pay-more-for-grid-infrastructure/)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**AI Server Boards Are Now Draining the PCB Supply Chain: TechPowerUp**
The Global Electronics Association, formerly IPC, warned that AI servers are taking board capacity and materials, TechPowerUp reported. North American PCB bookings are up 56.1 percent this year through September, while shipments have grown 13.3 percent. Lead times for high-layer boards are 16 to 20 weeks or more; the outlet said some PCB orders were taking up to 30 months, and that motherboard prices rose roughly 15 to 50 percent. A typical board has about 12 layers, while AI server boards are moving to 40 to 60 layers or more, so each board consumes more glass fabric, resin, copper foil, and laminate. At least $10 billion has gone into PCB plants in Southeast Asia and China over the past three years, and the association expects the shortage to last through at least the first half of 2027, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/355065/ai-server-boards-are-now-draining-the-pcb-supply-chain)

**US chip export curbs impact Alibaba Cloud, Tencent data center growth: ET Datacenters**
Alibaba Cloud expects reduced long-term data center expansion and capital-expenditure cuts as a new U.S. policy bans remote access to advanced AI chips, ET Datacenters reported. The same note says the Bureau of Industry and Security allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell 879,000 AI chips to military-linked Chinese entities, and that Alibaba and Tencent, listed as Chinese military companies, received approval for chip sales. Source: [datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com](https://datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/ai-compute-infrastructure/us-chip-export-curbs-impact-alibaba-cloud-tencent-data-center-growth/136043112?utm_source=latest_news&utm_medium=latestNews)

**YTL Power denies role in alleged Nvidia chip diversion to China, says US curbs will not affect data centres: The Malaysian Reserve**
YTL Power denies any role in an alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China, The Malaysian Reserve reported. The company says the U.S. curbs will not affect its data centres. Source: [themalaysianreserve.com](https://themalaysianreserve.com/2026/11/20/ytl-power-denies-role-in-alleged-nvidia-chip-diversion-to-china-says-us-curbs-will-not-affect-data-centres/)

### Also Today
**Gordon Bell Prize Goes to Chinese Team for Exascale FeMoco Solution: HPCwire**
A 10-member Chinese team won the ACM Gordon Bell Prize at SC26 for Closing the FeMo-Cofactor “Quantum-Advantage” Gap with Exascale Supercomputers, using conventional supercomputers on a quantum-chemistry problem. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/2026/11/20/gordon-bell-prize-goes-to-chinese-team-for-exascale-femoco-solution/)

**RIKEN Confirms Theft of 430 Private Keys in Fugaku and RIKYU Intrusion: HPCwire**
RIKEN now confirms theft of 430 private keys in the intrusion on the Fugaku and RIKYU supercomputers, after the November 18 warning of possible personal-data exposure. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/riken-confirms-theft-of-430-private-keys-in-fugaku-and-rikyu-intrusion/)

### The Teardown: Reading another PC's memory over USB4
Remote Direct Memory Access lets a workload on one machine touch memory on another without the usual copy through the operating system. Microsoft has turned that path on for Windows 11 over USB4, so several PCs can be daisy-chained and share a job. TechPowerUp's account of the work is a latency measurement, not a bandwidth bake-off, and the number that matters is how long a message takes to go and come back.

USB4 is the pipe, rated at up to 80 gigabits per second. Ethernet can already run over that same cable, and a UDP packet on that Ethernet path is the comparison Microsoft rejected. UDP still climbs the network stack: the message is wrapped, queued, copied, and unwrapped on the far side before the other PC's memory is involved. RDMA is built so the transfer lands in the other machine's memory with the CPU on that machine mostly out of the way. The engineering bet is that the stack, not the copper, was the wait.

The worked example is two PCs and a sweep of message size. TechPowerUp reports round-trip latency of 28 to 50 microseconds for RDMA over USB4. The same sweep on Ethernet over USB4 using UDP landed between 116 and 194 microseconds. At the fast end, 28 against 116; at the slow end, 50 against 194. The outlet calls the RDMA path roughly four times faster. Those four bounds are the whole published result: two machines, one cable family, two protocols, latency versus message size. The illustration of DGX Spark boxes linked by Ethernet is explicitly not this USB4 setup, so it does not add a third data point.

Eighty gigabits per second is the other limit, and it does not show up in a microsecond measurement of a short message. A short message finishes before the pipe is full, so the 28-to-50-microsecond access is what the user feels, and the 116-to-194-microsecond UDP path is the tax of the stack. Stretch the message and the bytes have to occupy that 80-gigabit USB4 pipe for longer, while the protocol gap stays in the same band the measurement already drew. Daisy-chained Windows 11 PCs stop being the right fabric when the job is limited by how many bytes that 80-gigabit pipe can move, not by the 28-to-50-microsecond memory access — a wider network then finishes the step, and the fourfold latency win no longer decides it. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/355062/microsoft-brings-rdma-over-usb4-to-windows-11-for-daisy-chained-pcs)

### On the Horizon
- First half of 2027: SpaceX lease schedules on the Vera Rubin notes begin when the GPUs and related equipment are delivered.
- First half of 2027 through mid-2028: the Global Electronics Association expects the PCB shortage to last through at least the first half of 2027, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028.
- Around 2028, and through 2029: major new memory fabs are not expected to add meaningful output before around 2028, while SK hynix says its HBM and related DRAM are sold out through 2029.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **TSMC halted Chinese foundry orders at sixteen nanometres and below without a US licence.**

**What You Need to Know:** TSMC has halted Chinese chip-design orders at 16 nanometres and below unless the customer gets a US export licence. Commerce rules that took effect Thursday also led Samsung to suspend some shipments, and they closed the path that let packaging firms clear designs without a case-by-case licence. Affected customers are generally held to 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes when the chips use neither high-bandwidth memory nor advanced packaging.

### Top Story
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing has told affected Chinese chip designers that orders at 16 nanometres and below are suspended unless a US export licence is in hand, and it said it will comply with the new US rule. The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security set the restrictions on November 16; they took effect Thursday, November 19, and they reach beyond AI processors. Samsung Electronics has also told Chinese customers that some processor shipments are paused while licences are sought, the Financial Times reported. The closed route was the one in which packaging and test firms checked a design and could ship without direct US approval. TSMC’s guidance generally limits those customers to 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, and only if the chips do not use high-bandwidth memory or advanced packaging. Advanced designs are now presumed to need a licence unless an exemption applies. TSMC will also review operating locations, parent companies, major shareholders, packaging providers, and shipping routes, including orders placed through subsidiaries or intermediaries in Taiwan, the United States, Europe, Japan, and Southeast Asia. A US list of approved designers names Nvidia, AMD, Apple, MediaTek, and Realtek, and no mainland Chinese companies. A separate source told Reuters that some Chinese AI chip designers could still use TSMC’s 7-nanometre process until November 19; Reuters could not independently verify that access. Samsung’s named Chinese customers include Baidu’s Kunlun unit and ByteDance. TSMC supplies smartphone processors to Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo; an exemption that had covered chips designed for non-AI uses such as smartphones is gone, and an industry official predicted Commerce would likely approve smartphone chips while warning that the process could delay production. Source: [businesstoday.com.my](https://www.businesstoday.com.my/2026/11/20/tsmc-tightens-china-chip-restrictions-following-new-us-export-rules/)
Source: [asiae.co.kr](https://www.asiae.co.kr/en/article/2026112008442479237)
Source: [finance.yahoo.com](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/tsmc-halts-advanced-chip-orders-000631441.html)

### Silicon
**Nvidia announces a Rubin HPC GPU and a Vera rack at SC26: Semiconductor Engineering**
At SC26 in Chicago, Nvidia announced a Rubin HPC GPU with more than 50,000 CUDA cores on a single GPU, plus sparse data acceleration. It also announced a 192-CPU Vera rack-scale platform for HPC with more than 200 TB/s of aggregate peak memory bandwidth. Both are conference announcements, not a statement that the parts have shipped. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-165/)

**Penguin Solutions unveils a photonic memory appliance: HPCwire**
Penguin Solutions announced MemoryAI Photonic Appliance at SC26. The company describes a photonics-based, HBM-class memory appliance, using Marvell technology, so CPUs and GPUs can share memory across servers. It is an unveiling, not a reported deployment. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/2026/11/19/penguin-solutions-turns-to-silicon-photonics-to-overcome-hpc-and-ai-memory-bottlenecks/)

**Nvidia and Microsoft put Vera Rubin NVL72 into Azure: BigGo Finance**
Microsoft and Nvidia described Azure’s adoption of Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, tuned for large-scale training, inference, and agentic applications, with Nvidia Confidential Computing on the racks. Signal65 benchmark data cited by the companies say Azure scaled to 10,240 Nvidia GPUs in MLPerf Training v6.1 and led cloud submissions in MLPerf Inference v6.1, with more than 10 percent higher throughput on DeepSeek-R1. Microsoft’s custom Cobalt 200, aimed at agentic workloads, delivers up to 50 percent better performance than Cobalt 100, while Microsoft keeps buying outside silicon. On buildout, management’s order is self-built facilities first, then long-term leases in which Microsoft controls fit-out, networking, and hardware; cancellations of some third-party orders were attributed to supplier delivery shortfalls, not a change in that order. Satya Nadella said Azure has surpassed $100 billion in revenue. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/1cadf87c-2194-4cc6-92b0-fbc0a8d2b6c6)

### Data Centres & Power
**AI data-centre power demand set to double by 2030: Tom's Hardware**
Tom’s Hardware, citing an IEA report, says AI data-centre power demand will double by 2030 on the back of $4 trillion in spending, a load it compares to adding an entire Great Britain of energy strain. The same account cites 93 large AI factories with projected capacity of around 50 gigawatts, and says power production and distribution are barely keeping up with that growth. This is a forecast in a report, not an energized site. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/data-centers/ai-data-center-power-demand-will-double-by-2030-thanks-to-usd4-trillion-in-spending-adding-an-entire-great-britain-to-energy-strain-93-large-ai-factories-with-projected-capacity-of-around-50-gigawatts)

**Bull holds the top three Green500 places: HPCwire**
At SC26 in Chicago, Bull systems held the top three places on the Green500 for a third straight edition of the ranking. HPCwire reported that those three are the world’s most energy-efficient supercomputers in the latest list, alongside Bull’s presence on the TOP500. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/bull-systems-hold-top-3-green500-spots-for-third-straight-edition/)

**Ecolab convenes a liquid-cooling ecosystem: Semiconductor Digest**
Ecolab announced it is convening an open AI-infrastructure ecosystem aimed at faster development of next-generation data centres, framed in the announcement as a liquid-cooling ecosystem for more efficient AI infrastructure. The step is an industry convening, not a commissioned cooling plant. Source: [semiconductor-digest.com](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/ecolab-launches-liquid-cooling-ecosystem-to-shape-the-industrys-most-efficient-ai-infrastructure/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=ecolab-launches-liquid-cooling-ecosystem-to-shape-the-industrys-most-efficient-ai-infrastructure)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**GlobalFoundries breaks ground on a 300 mm fab in Malta: Semiconductor Engineering**
GlobalFoundries broke ground on a new 300 mm semiconductor fab in Malta, New York, under a US-Japan investment initiative providing up to $21 billion for two fabs. The first 300 mm fab is expected to begin production in 2029. Ground has been broken; production has not started. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-165/)

**Commerce tightens remote access and logs China chip licences: Semiconductor Engineering**
The US Commerce Department introduced new restrictions on remote access to advanced US AI computing through overseas data centres, and new semiconductor licensing requirements affecting Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. US government data cited in the same review say the United States received licence requests covering 3.4 million advanced Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China and approved more than 879,000. How many of the approved chips were actually shipped is unclear in that account. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-165/)

**TSMC Partners completes a $500 million Anthropic purchase: Open Magazine**
TSMC’s board had authorised up to $500 million each in Anthropic common shares and OpenAI preferred stock on November 10; a filing now shows the Anthropic purchase is done, while the OpenAI authorisation is not confirmation of a completed buy. TSMC Partners acquired 6,024,096 Anthropic shares for about $500 million at $83 a share, the IPO price, about 0.03 percent at an IPO valuation of about $1.5 trillion. Anthropic opened on November 19 at $111.50 and closed at $97.17, which Open Magazine calculates as a paper value of about $585.4 million, an unrealised gain of about $85.4 million, or 17.1 percent. The filing does not establish an exclusive chip-supply agreement, and the gain is not a reported sale. Source: [openthemagazine.com](https://openthemagazine.com/technology/quick-take-500-million-for-just-003-of-anthropic-seven-things-to-know-about-tsmcs-bet)

### Also Today
**Boston Dynamics and GlobalFoundries expand Spot deployments: Semiconductor Digest**
Boston Dynamics and GlobalFoundries said they are expanding Spot autonomous inspection across GF fabs in the United States, Germany, and Singapore. Source: [semiconductor-digest.com](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/boston-dynamics-globalfoundries-expand-robotics-collaboration/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=boston-dynamics-globalfoundries-expand-robotics-collaboration)

**Seasonic teases a 3,200 W enterprise supply: TechPowerUp**
Seasonic posted that its 3,200 W Prime Enterprise PX-3200, with six 12V-2x6 connectors and 80 Plus Platinum and Cybernetics Platinum ratings, is coming soon; at Computex 2026 two of the units powered a system with four Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell cards. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/355047/seasonic-teases-imminent-launch-of-3-200-w-prime-enterprise-px-3200-psu)

### The Teardown: The Rack That Outgrew Ten Kilowatts
A GPU server changes the colocation decision at the electrical service, before lease rate or city enters the comparison. Data Center Knowledge sets the older test as location, how much infrastructure was going in, and how the operator expected to grow. Those questions remain. What moved is how much of the answer is now owned by power delivery, heat removal, the wait for a utility interconnection, and whether the accelerators stay busy enough to earn their cost.

The mechanism is density stacked on duty cycle. Power density is not a larger number on the same busbar. A rack that draws several times a conventional load needs feeders, breakers, and a cooling path sized for that rack, then a contract for the energy, then a utility willing to interconnect on a timeline the project can survive. Utilization sits on top of that physics. Accelerator servers cost enough that an idle machine is a capital loss, so a hall built for a peak and left dark between runs fails the return test even when the megawatts exist on paper.

Walk the figures Data Center Knowledge actually gives, as a planning case rather than a measured hall. The historical ceiling it states is no more than about 10 kilowatts for a typical rack. GPU-enabled servers, it says, push that figure higher, often by a factor of ten. Ten times about 10 kilowatts is about 100 kilowatts at the rack — the article’s multiplier applied to the article’s ceiling, not a vendor nameplate and not a utility filing. That product is the load the power train, the cooling plant, and the interconnection request have to be ready for if the “often” case is the one you design to. The second figure in the piece splits the fleet, not the wattage. If only 10 percent of planned servers will include GPUs, GPU-specific power and cooling need not decide the whole campus. The other share of the plan can still turn on cost structure, location, and room to expand. The article’s contrast is binary after that: once GPUs are a substantial portion of the environment, power and cooling become central. It does not publish the percentage at which “substantial” begins, so the worked line stops at the 10 percent case it does publish.

Duty cycle then chooses the owner of the hall. For training, where demand may be bursty rather than constant, Data Center Knowledge argues colocation can be the cheaper path: deploy in a building already equipped for high density rather than fund a GPU-ready private hall that sits idle for long stretches. For GPU-intensive work that runs continuously, such as large-scale inference, the private hall can win over time if the operator buys power more cheaply than a colocation provider that builds a markup into the power price. The higher upfront capital is then a bid to cut operating cost, not a bid to arrive sooner. Speed runs the other direction. A new private data centre can take years, longer if permitting slips, and a finished building can still wait on utility power. In many markets, the piece says, grid interconnection timelines are now a major constraint. A colocation provider that already holds power capacity, cooling, and staff can bring the same dense racks up sooner.

Sustainability follows the same pipe, because the accelerators consume far more power than conventional infrastructure and so raise the stakes on the mix behind the meter. Colocation can be the nearer path to renewables when the provider already holds renewable contracts, a low-carbon mix, or offsets. Matching that in a private hall is harder where renewable supply is limited or on-site generation is impractical. An aggressive sustainability target can therefore pick the landlord even when the long-run power price would have favoured owning the building.

The private build stops being the right choice when the accelerator share is large, the workload is bursty, and the interconnection is measured in years rather than in capacity a provider already holds. In that case the capital buys a dense hall that waits — on the utility, and on the next training run — while a colocation contract rents density that is already energized. The private hall fits again only when the GPUs run continuously and the operator’s own power price undercuts the provider’s markup by enough to repay those years of construction. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/colocation/how-gpus-are-changing-the-colocation-vs-private-data-center-debate)

### On the Horizon
- Siemens’ acquisition of Breker Verification Systems is expected to close in December.
- GlobalFoundries plans to begin evaluating Boston Dynamics Atlas humanoid robots for fab tasks in early 2027.
- A public preview of GPU-accelerated Direct Stream for Windows 365 Cloud PCs, up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second, is expected in early 2027.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **JEDEC previews DDR6 at 12.8 GT/s, quadrupling DDR5 module bandwidth.**

**What You Need to Know:** JEDEC's DDR6 preview sets a 12.8 GT/s baseline and 153.6 GB/s per module, four times DDR5's 38.4 GB/s, on a module cut from 133 mm to 74 mm. TrendForce now has NAND contract prices turning down from the first quarter of 2027 after Chinese cloud SSD cuts outweigh North American order growth. A Fluke survey of 500 U.S. operators finds power quality inside the building, not only the grid interconnect, already limiting GPU rollouts.

### Top Story
JEDEC has previewed DDR6, and Tom's Hardware reports the baseline transfer rate at 12,800 MT/s against DDR5's 4,800 MT/s and DDR4's 1,600 MT/s. Baseline bandwidth per module is 153.6 GB/s, against 38.4 GB/s for DDR5 and 12.8 GB/s for DDR4 — a fourfold lift versus DDR5's baseline, from a 96-bit bus split into four 24-bit sub-channels rather than DDR5's two 32-bit sub-channels. Peak JEDEC rates in the preview table are 14,400 MT/s and 172.8 GB/s per module, against DDR5's peak of 9,200 MT/s and 73.6 GB/s. Modules are specified at 74 mm, 44 percent shorter than the 133 mm DDR5 and DDR4 modules, and only about 6 percent longer than a DDR5 SO-DIMM. Bank count doubles to 64. DDR6 is described as supporting 128 Gb (16 GB) dies, four times the density of early DDR5, with through-silicon-via stacking; Tom's Hardware writes that server RDIMMs could scale to 1 TB or more per slot, against 512 GB reached on server DDR5 RDIMMs and 64 GB on current consumer DDR5 modules. On the server side, RDIMMs are described as starting at DDR6-12800, where DDR5 RDIMMs topped out at DDR5-9200. Potential form factors named in the preview include RDIMM, UDIMM, and CAMM. Tom's Hardware says many believe 2029 is a realistic commercialization target, and that JEDEC has no official launch date. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/ram/ddr6-ram-shrinks-by-44-percent-while-delivering-4x-ddr5s-baseline-bandwidth-jedec-previews-12-8-gt-s-modules-with-up-to-1-terabyte-of-capacity-per-slot)

### Silicon
**MSI unveils the EdgeMesa N AI+ Series: TechPowerUp**
MSI has introduced the EdgeMesa N AI+ Series, a compact desktop it says is powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark, as an announced system rather than a stated shipment. The chassis is 1.3 litres of aluminium. MSI's AI Pulse cooling, with a vapor chamber and dual turbo fans, is described as sustaining 140 W TDP and 24/7 agent operation. At the core, the NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X superchip combines a 6,144-core NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance, and up to 128 GB of LPDDR5X unified memory, with CUDA. Connectivity listed in the release is 10 Gb LAN, Wi-Fi 7, 20 Gbps USB-C, and up to four displays. NVIDIA Personal AI Router is described as routing independent inference requests across compatible local nodes. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/355023/msi-unveils-the-edgemesa-n-ai-series-powering-the-future-of-ai-teammates)

**Kulicke & Soffa ships fluxless thermo-compression bonders: Semiconductor Digest**
Kulicke & Soffa has shipped what it calls the industry's first fluxless thermo-compression bonding systems for substrate-level packaging, to two separate major customers in Taiwan. The company frames the shipment as an acceleration of panel-level capability for AI applications. This is a shipment, not a roadmap slide. Source: [semiconductor-digest.com](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/kulicke-soffa-accelerates-industry-shift-to-panel-level-capability-for-ai-applications/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=kulicke-soffa-accelerates-industry-shift-to-panel-level-capability-for-ai-applications)

**AMD's data-center mix versus the gamer post: TechPowerUp**
AMD posted record Q3 2026 revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45 percent year over year, TechPowerUp reports. Data Center brought in a record $8.5 billion, 64 percent of total revenue, up 97 percent year over year. Client and Gaming fell 8 percent to $3.7 billion; Client grew 7 percent, so the drop sits in Gaming, down 40 percent to $773 million, under 6 percent of total revenue. AMD expects data-center sales to grow roughly 50 percent from Q3 to Q4. Less than two weeks earlier, CEO Lisa Su called AMD a data-center-first company. Tom's Hardware, citing the earnings call, reports she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027, data-center AI revenue to grow faster than that, data center to be more than 80 percent of total revenue in 2027, and PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage in 2027. AMD Japan's post saying the company values gamers above all else drew a community note pointing at that split. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/355012/amds-we-love-gamers-post-clashes-with-its-own-ceos-comments)

**EuroHPC: JUPITER ranks fifth on the TOP500: HPCwire**
The November 2026 TOP500 and Green500, released at Supercomputing 2026, place JUPITER fifth, and among the world's ten most powerful systems. HPCwire reports that all operational EuroHPC supercomputers are on the TOP500 again. Preparations are progressing for Alice Recoque, described as Europe's second exascale system, with arrival in 2027. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/eurohpc-prepares-for-alice-recoque-as-jupiter-ranks-5th-on-the-top500/)

**Microsoft will use Intel EMIB for Azure silicon: Tech Times**
Microsoft and Intel on November 18 announced an expansion of their collaboration under a long-term agreement to develop differentiated Azure capabilities and system-level optimizations for cloud and AI. Tech Times reports Microsoft will use Intel EMIB packaging for Azure silicon. Source: [techtimes.com](https://www.techtimes.com/articles/331034/20261118/microsoft-will-use-intel-emib-packaging-azure-silicon-release-omits-chip-date.htm)

### Data Centres & Power
**AI workloads hit by power-quality issues: Data Center Knowledge**
A Fluke survey of 500 U.S. data-center operators and professionals, reported by Data Center Knowledge, finds electrical problems constraining AI deployments inside facilities that may already have grid power. Nearly a third said power-quality issues have reduced their ability to deploy or operate high-density AI and GPU workloads. Just 36 percent said their electrical infrastructure is fully prepared for higher-density AI workloads, while 74 percent said insufficient power and grid capacity are moderately or severely limiting expansion. About 76 percent reported electrical or power-system issues. Separately, 79 percent said power-quality problems had contributed over the past year to delays, service disruptions, unplanned downtime, or serious near-misses — a grouping that includes incidents that did not become outages. Some 78 percent said they lacked comprehensive, continuous, real-time visibility across critical electrical systems, and 15 percent said electrical problems were identified only after performance degradation, equipment failure, or downtime. Recruiting qualified electrical technicians has become harder for 57 percent; 65 percent said skills shortages had not delayed infrastructure upgrades or new capacity. Fluke's Michael Stuart told Data Center Knowledge the risk is whether internal infrastructure can distribute power at scale, and that harmonics, voltage sags and swells, thermal hotspots, cooling, and undocumented connections show up where power, cooling, and cabling meet. He recommends measuring power quality as close as possible to the GPU loads before deployment. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/energy-power-supply/ai-workloads-hit-by-power-quality-issues-at-data-centers)

**Hai Long 2A ends its Taipower tariff to sell to TSMC: BigGo Finance**
Taiwan's Hai Long 2A wind farm is ending its Taipower feed-in tariff arrangement in order to sell power to TSMC, BigGo Finance reports. Taiwan's Energy Administration says the change will save Taipower NT$44 billion over 20 years. This is a reported offtake shift, not a new groundbreaking. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/741e986a-08ae-4da0-9d46-f6ac24befcd7)

**CoreWeave cites a Signal65 price-and-performance study: CoreWeave**
CoreWeave said a Signal65 study found a token served on CoreWeave costs up to 65 percent less than on three hyperscalers, and that on price alone CoreWeave is 22 percent under the most competitively priced of those hyperscalers. The company attributes the rest to GPUs on bare metal with no hypervisor, over a 1:1 nonblocking fabric. For a team serving DeepSeek-R1 on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72, it said $1 million a year buys up to 2.9 times as many tokens. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/CoreWeave/status/2123140448780750882)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**NAND contract prices set to decline in 2027: TechPowerUp**
TrendForce forecasts that overall NAND Flash contract prices will begin declining in the first quarter of 2027, by 0 to 5 percent quarter on quarter, with all product categories entering a downward cycle from the second quarter as quarterly drops potentially widen. It estimates global NAND industry capital expenditure will rise 26.7 percent year over year to $29.9 billion in 2027, and that bit supply will still grow 25 to 30 percent year over year even if some suppliers slow expansion. North American cloud providers have raised 2027 demand forecasts again, on AI-agent and general-purpose server projects already under construction. Chinese cloud providers, facing GPU shortages, elevated inventory, and token-price competition, have cut 2027 enterprise SSD orders by more than the additional U.S. demand. TrendForce has already lowered its fourth-quarter 2026 contract-price increase forecast to 8 to 13 percent. Spot prices recently corrected by more than 20 percent. It flags Chinese inventory drawdown, overseas GPU-procurement restrictions, lower device memory specifications into 2028, and U.S. policy after the midterms — including 2028 AI data-center projects still in planning and permitting — as the variables for second-half 2027 buying. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/355022/nand-flash-prices-set-to-decline-in-2027-as-chinese-csp-order-cuts-outweigh-north-american-demand-growth)

**Packaging and foundry called Korea's next HBM problem: BigGo Finance**
At the 2026 Global Future Technology Forum on November 18, hosted by Korea Economic TV, U.S. and Japanese specialists argued Samsung and SK Hynix cannot hold an HBM edge on the memory die alone. Paul Triolo of DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group called advanced packaging, plus logic and memory interface capability, South Korea's top priority, and said next-generation HBM is as much a packaging and foundry problem as a memory problem. Takashi Yunogami of Japan's Micro Processing Research Institute said 2.5D packaging, which places GPUs and HBM side by side on an interposer, is a near-80 percent TSMC monopoly, and that without it dramatic success will be difficult. Triolo said Chinese companies have already surpassed the technical benchmarks set for logic and memory, and that Chinese domestic equipment share rose from about 5 percent before 2022 to 20 to 30 percent depending on segment. Douglas Fuller of Copenhagen Business School argued lithography access can constrain China's DRAM chase, while NAND warrants more vigilance toward YMTC; views on CXMT diverged between long-term limits and today's volume threat. Yunogami said Rapidus has no foundation in intermediate process generations, that IBM GAA technology alone is not enough for mass production, and that he believes Rapidus mass-producing 2-nanometer semiconductors is impossible. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/a308582e-4ed0-4b83-9768-460a1d1df6c1)

**Johnson backs tighter AI chip export limits: NOLA.com**
The comments came the same day Jensen Huang announced his resignation, after The New York Times reported an affair with a tech executive U.S. intelligence deemed a Chinese spy, and after another reported relationship with a staffer. Democrats won control of Congress in the November 3 midterms and take over in January. A spokesperson for Majority Leader Steve Scalise said he is working with the White House so export-control text does not unduly tie the administration's hands or unintentionally take billions out of the American economy. President Trump, whose portfolio NOLA.com says includes Nvidia stock, has supported Huang and called for his reinstatement. The U.S. already bars Nvidia's most advanced chips to China while permitting some lower-level chips. This week the administration backed rules that restrict remote access to advanced AI chips and make them harder for Southeast Asian countries to obtain. Three bills — the MATCH Act, the AI Overwatch Act, and the Chip Security Act — cleared the House Foreign Affairs Committee in the first half of the year and were never debated by the full House, according to Riki Parikh of the Alliance for Secure AI. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks want chip-export limits in the National Defense Authorization Act; the House passed a July version without them, and the Senate has not passed its version. A Johnson spokesperson did not say which restrictions he supports. Parikh said that if Republicans do not pass restrictions by year-end, Democrats are likely to pursue them in January, with Warren slated to chair Senate Banking. Source: [nola.com](https://www.nola.com/news/mike-johnson-ai-chips-nvidia/article_72ddd6a2-3645-4e78-9f05-3de77a9498ba.html)

### Also Today
**Phison AI Data Platform brings on-premises generative BI: HPCwire**
Phison launched the Phison AI Data Platform with generative business intelligence, a sovereign on-premises system powered by Pascari aiDAPTIV cache memory, and is showing it at Supercomputing 2026 booth 5413. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/phison-ai-data-platform-brings-sovereign-on-premises-generative-bi-to-enterprises/)

**From metrology to autonomy: Semiconductor Engineering**
Intel Foundry leaders used 14 presentations and posters at SEMICON West 2026 to argue factory autonomy needs trusted metrology, and the SATAS consortium — more than 40 organizations, sponsored by Japan's NEDO and METI — is writing open back-end automation standards. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/from-metrology-to-autonomy-scaling-yield-quality-and-innovation/)

### The Teardown: The Recipe Space an Etcher Actually Has
An etch step is a point picked from RF power, chamber pressure, gas chemistry, temperature, and time, and moving one of those knobs changes more than one thing the metrology will later score. Critical dimension can tighten while a film somewhere else in the stack thins, or a profile that looked clean at one pressure bows once the incoming wafer is a little different. Semiconductor Engineering's account of SEMICON West 2026, drawing on Lam Research and Intel Foundry, treats that as a search problem before it is a machine-learning problem: the tool already exposes a space no engineer can walk by habit.

David Fried of Lam Research's Semiverse group described, on a panel, how a process engineer looking at a data set reaches for the region that worked a decade ago — lower pressure, higher power — because that is the bias the last fix left behind. The current Lam Research etcher he described has a potential recipe space on the order of 10²³ combinations. That is not a menu of twenty-three settings. It is the product of every knob the recipe can turn, each with its own legal range, multiplied out. A human team samples the neighborhoods it already trusts. An optimizer that is allowed to ignore that history can land in an operating region the team would not have opened, because the interactions were not visible in the plots they were used to reading.

Intel's side of the same problem, from Vikas Sharma of Intel Foundry R&D, is larger still and already has a clock on it. One process he discussed has 350 parameters and about 10⁷⁰⁰ theoretical combinations. Engineers working with the equipment suppliers spent about a year getting a minimally acceptable recipe for that tool and that layer, then kept working with limited success. After AI-assisted optimization they were finding better results within a few months, and more than one of those results beat the original baseline. The search did not stop at "better." Sharma's point, as reported, is that AI could identify thousands of candidates, and each one still had to be judged with silicon experiments that are expensive. Parameters in that space are nonlinear: a relationship that holds in one corner of the recipe does not hold in another, so a model tuned on the first corner mis-ranks the second.

Two recipes can hit the same performance point in development and then diverge once the line is real. Sharma's framing is stability, not the hero number: minor perturbations in incoming material or at the tool can drop performance sharply. Fried's separate caution is that there is no single AI method for every layer. Full physical simulation, surrogate models, machine learning, deep learning, large language models, and agentic setups each cover a different job — exploring conditions versus coordinating the engineering workflow — and the time is going into choosing which form addresses which workflow, not into declaring the search finished. Handing one model's recommendation to the next model imports the first model's assumptions whether or not anyone wrote them down.

Inspection is the place this already touches production, and advanced packaging is where the count gets physical. Some packages contain hundreds of thousands of interconnects, each a possible open or short. Automated optical inspection and X-ray collect the images; machine learning can separate shades a person reads as one gray. Ingu Yin Chang of ASE put that at a thousand shades of gray against the few a human eye sorts. Finding the shade is not the same as authorizing a process change. The candidate still has to be a defect, not a tolerable variation, before anyone moves a knob.

The design choice — let the optimizer nominate the recipe, then confirm it on wafers — stops being the right one when the nominated point is only stable inside the slice of incoming material and tool condition the model saw. Nonlinear regions mean a ranking earned in one corner does not travel. Thousands of candidates against a silicon budget means most of the 10²³, and essentially all of the 10⁷⁰⁰, will never be run. Authority to change the line belongs to the experiment that still fails the perturbation, not to the search that found the point. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/can-ai-make-its-own-manufacturing-decisions/)

### On the Horizon
- Alice Recoque, Europe's second exascale system, is being prepared for arrival in 2027, alongside JUPITER's fifth-place November 2026 TOP500 ranking.
- TrendForce has NAND Flash contract prices beginning a decline in the first quarter of 2027, 0 to 5 percent quarter on quarter, with every product category in a downward cycle from the second quarter.
- Lawmakers including Warren and Banks want AI-chip export language in the defense authorization bill, and Parikh said that if the Republican-led Congress does not pass restrictions by the end of 2026, Democrats are likely to take them up in January.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **More than 3.5 times the substrate capacity for Nvidia starts in 2027, binding six manufacturers to the ramp.**

**What You Need to Know:** Kinsus will expand advanced ABF package-substrate capacity dedicated to Nvidia by more than 3.5 times at its Youth campus in Taoyuan, with production expected to begin in the second half of 2027. The same set of commitments pulls in Amkor, Foxconn, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SPIL and TSMC across substrates, packaging, wafers and system assembly. Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs began volume shipments in the third quarter on TSMC’s 5nm, 3nm and CoWoS.

### Top Story
Nvidia is locking manufacturing capacity to demand for its accelerated-computing platforms through expanded agreements with Amkor Technology, Foxconn, Kinsus Interconnect Technology, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and TSMC, covering substrates, advanced packaging, wafer manufacturing, contract manufacturing and system assembly. Kinsus plans to expand advanced ABF package-substrate capacity dedicated to Nvidia by more than 3.5 times at its Youth campus in Taoyuan, Taiwan, with production expected to begin in the second half of 2027. Nvidia is backing Amkor’s advanced-packaging expansion in Arizona and South Korea through multiyear agreements announced in July and October 2026, totalling nearly $3 billion and including prepayments. In Taiwan, a multiyear SPIL agreement backed by multibillion-dollar funding covers bumping, interposer wafer fabrication, assembly and testing; Digitimes reports that deal is set to triple advanced packaging capacity by 2029. Samsung Electro-Mechanics amended an existing substrate agreement to improve factory operations in South Korea, building on work in Sejong and Busan for computing and high-speed networking, while Foxconn is extending collaboration on next-generation GPU and networking platforms across Asia, North America and Europe. Nvidia said Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs began volume shipments in the third quarter, using TSMC’s 5nm, 3nm and CoWoS advanced packaging. Source: [yourstory.com](https://yourstory.com/ai-story/nvidia-chip-supply-partnerships-ai-demand) · [digitimes.com](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20261118PD239/nvidia-spil-packaging-capacity.html)

### Silicon
**Vera Rubin Rack Power: Penguin Solutions Launch Gives No kW Figure, Lenovo Lists 227 kW: Tech Times**
Lenovo lists a Vera Rubin rack at 227 kW. Tech Times set that figure against Penguin Solutions’ Vera Rubin rack launch. Source: [techtimes.com](https://www.techtimes.com/articles/330989/20261118/vera-rubin-rack-power-penguin-solutions-launch-gives-no-kw-figure-lenovo-lists-227-kw.htm)

**Taiwan Mask expands 14-inch capacity to capture CoWoS and photonics growth: digitimes**
Taiwan Mask, a subsidiary of Star Fusion Group, is expanding 14-inch capacity while overhauling its product mix and expanding overseas. Digitimes said the push is aimed at demand across advanced packaging, including CoWoS, silicon photonics and advanced-node photomasks. Source: [digitimes.com](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20261118PD253/taiwan-mask-growth-photonics-14-inch-capacity.html)

**QUDORA Adds NVIDIA CUDA-Q Support to Its Qamelion Quantum Emulator: HPCwire**
QUDORA Technologies, founded in 2021 and based in Braunschweig, has integrated NVIDIA CUDA-Q into its SDK so developers can run hybrid programs on Qamelion, an emulator with adaptive noise modeling of the company’s upcoming trapped-ion hardware. Its Near Field Quantum Control technology uses integrated microwave electronics to control trapped-ion qubits in an architecture the company says is compatible with standard semiconductor manufacturing. The CUDA-Q integration is available now; QUDORA offers systems for on-premises installation and cloud access, and is expanding in Asia-Pacific through QUDORA Japan K.K. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/qudora-adds-nvidia-cuda-q-support-to-its-qamelion-quantum-emulator/)

### Data Centres & Power
**Taiwan completes Asia's largest single offshore wind project off central coast, connecting 1 GW of capacity to supply TSMC in 2027: digitimes**
Taiwan’s Hai Long Offshore Wind Project is energized off the central coast: construction is complete and all 73 turbines are connected to the grid, for 1 GW of capacity. Digitimes said that capacity is to supply TSMC in 2027. Source: [digitimes.com](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20261118PD227/taiwan-offshore-wind-capacity-tsmc-2027.html)

**Public Pushback Complicates Data Center Buildouts: Data Center Knowledge**
Community resistance is forcing developers to reassess permits, tax benefits and utility arrangements, including in states that had courted the projects. In Pennsylvania, gubernatorial candidate Stacy Garrity moved from praising Amazon’s $20 billion data-center investment to backing a pause and stronger requirements, and Gov. Josh Shapiro moved from promoting faster permitting to supporting stricter environmental standards and transparency, Spotlight PA reported. Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley backed a pause and elimination of the industry’s state sales-tax exemption, and after the election said he was considering resource-use disclosures, community-support requirements and protections against shifting energy costs onto residents. GlobalData found that projects breaking ground between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026 waited an average of just over two years from announcement to construction, up from about 18 months for projects launched between early 2020 and mid-2025. IDC’s Sreenivas Duvvuri Venkata said community acceptance now sits with power, interconnection and environmental permits as a condition of timely execution, and that conditions can include full utility-cost responsibility, renewable requirements, closed-loop cooling and limits to designated industrial sites. Alston Mason of Oldcastle Infrastructure said a site can have its power plan set and still be waiting on environmental permits for on-site generation equipment. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/public-pushback-complicates-data-center-buildouts)

**$3.26 million in SpaceX AI data center revenue will be pumped back into the City of Memphis: Tom's Hardware**
Memphis is making its first major outlay under the Community Benefit Ordinance, allocating $3,259,282 from tax revenue on SpaceX AI’s Colossus 1, which has been operating since May 2025. Of that, $2 million goes to the Memphis HOPE home-repair program, offering low- and moderate-income homeowners and renters up to $25,000 as a deferred, interest-free, forgivable loan with zero monthly payments, forgiven after three years, and $125,000 is set for cooling and air-quality equipment for residents. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/data-centers/usd3-26-million-in-spacex-ai-data-center-revenue-will-be-pumped-back-into-the-city-of-memphis-up-to-usd25-000-on-offer-to-low-income-residents-for-repairs-and-home-improvements)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**NVIDIA's Supply Chain Chief Deb Shoquist: Allocating TSMC Chips Weekly, Delivery Cycles Can Be Compressed to Two Weeks: BigGo Finance**
Deb Shoquist, Nvidia’s executive vice president of operations, described a supplier screen of three conditions — ramp cadence that matches Nvidia, technical precision for complex designs, and the balance sheet to invest ahead — and said Nvidia will inject capital if a partner has only two of the three. The network she named runs through TSMC (a partner since 1998), Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, KYEC (packaging and test partners for more than two decades), Unimicron, Amphenol, Coherent and Lumentum; she meets major suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks a year on the road in Taiwan, mainland China, South Korea, Vietnam and the United States. Optics partners had technology but not the factory scale Nvidia needed, which is why Nvidia entered investment partnerships with Coherent and Lumentum, and why co-packaged optics is being built as a new supply chain. Amphenol’s cable assembly has 1,500 branches, each assembled to keep the defect rate below one per million, on more than a hundred automated lines in Vietnam, and is now in full production. Wafers are allocated weekly after packaging: a plant with low output or a short holding period does not get more chips that week, and every die is traced from its identification number to the customer invoice. When required, the cycle from chips leaving TSMC to systems shipping from Foxconn and Wistron can be cut from five weeks to two. On one compute-board ramp, automated test-handling throughput came in below plan; the line was paused, manual loading was restored with as many as several hundred operators, and an internal effort called Swarm redesigned tray, hardware, software and yield issues with Foxconn’s automation engineers before scaling resumed. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/61a48295-5190-4c04-9e2f-e1af9e0bb715)

**S’pore can facilitate US checks on AI chip use, won’t allow circumvention of export controls: PM Wong: The Straits Times**
A day after the November 16 licensing rule, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on November 17 that Singapore can facilitate US checks on how advanced chips are deployed in the city-state, will not enforce another country’s export controls, and will take clear and firm action against firms that use Singapore to circumvent them. He said only a small volume of chips recorded as Singapore sales actually enter the country; 2025 statistics showed Nvidia reporting Singapore as 22 percent of global chip-sales revenue while only 1 percent of the chips were used there. The same day, Minister Josephine Teo and US Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler agreed to follow up on practical arrangements for continued trusted access, which Singapore’s digital-development ministry confirmed on November 18, and Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Singapore will act against those who flout its laws. China’s Ministry of Commerce said on November 17 that the tighter controls run counter to the leaders’ consensus and that China will take countermeasures if the US persists; Zaobao reported that overseas data centres providing substantial computing capacity to companies headquartered in China must obtain a US export licence within 90 days or face further restrictions, with applications reviewed case by case. The Commerce rule requires a licence to export, re-export or transfer advanced semiconductors to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. Source: [straitstimes.com](https://www.straitstimes.com/asia/spore-can-facilitate-us-checks-on-ai-chip-use-wont-allow-circumvention-of-export-controls-pm-wong) · [zaobao.com.sg](https://www.zaobao.com.sg/en/news/china/china-says-tighter-us-ai-chip-export-controls-undermine-international-trade-order) · [businesstoday.com.my](https://www.businesstoday.com.my/2026/11/18/singapore-seeks-us-assurances-to-keep-advanced-chip-access-open)

### Also Today
**Lambda Touts First CPO Deployment of Blackwell GPUs: HPCwire**
HPCwire reported Lambda’s claim of the first co-packaged-optics deployment of Blackwell GPUs. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/2026/11/17/lambda-touts-first-cpo-deployment-of-blackwell-gpus/)

**RIKEN Warns Fugaku and RIKYU Users of Possible Personal Data Exposure: HPCwire**
RIKEN said unauthorized access to a system involved in operating the Fugaku supercomputer was confirmed on November 13, with a possible personal-information leak affecting Fugaku and RIKYU users. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/riken-warns-fugaku-and-rikyu-users-of-possible-personal-data-exposure/)

**Jensen Huang Will Not Be Reinstated as CEO, Says NVIDIA Board Chief: TechPowerUp**
Board chairman Harvey Jones said on the third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call that the board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation and does not intend to reinstate him as CEO. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/354967/jensen-huang-will-not-be-reinstated-as-ceo-says-nvidia-board-chief)

**Nvidia Introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang for Workaround on U.S. Export Controls: The Information**
The Information reported that Nvidia introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang for a workaround on US export controls. Source: [theinformation.com](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/nvidia-introduced-alibaba-alice-huang-workaround-u-s-export-controls)

**TSMC reportedly demands cash up front from AI chip clients amid circular financing fears: investingLive**
investingLive reported that TSMC is demanding cash up front from AI chip clients amid fears of circular financing. Source: [investinglive.com](https://investinglive.com/news/tsmc-reportedly-demands-cash-up-front-from-ai-chip-clients-amid-circular-financing-fears/)

### The Teardown: The Film Between the Resin and the Mold
Release film is the sheet that keeps epoxy off the tool. In compression molding for IC packaging, hot resin is pressed around the die and the substrate. If that resin wets the mold, the next shot is contaminated and the demold can tear the package. BigGo Finance, reporting chairman Yang Yun-pin’s pre-listing presentation, describes Suregiant’s film as the layer that isolates epoxy from the mold under high temperature and high pressure so the part releases clean.

The process choice is how the film is made. Yang said Japanese peers mostly extrude film. Suregiant coats it, drawing on more than 25 years of precision coating and formulation, from an optoelectronics start that entered semiconductors in 2014. Coating is what lets a supplier cut a custom sample for one customer’s automated line. The line cares about three outcomes: non-stick sheeting, no adhesive residue, and a release force that matches the tool. An extruded film can post the same force number and still fail if the surface chemistry is not the one that mold, resin and cycle were qualified against. The sample, not a catalog roll, is the product.

The package stack changed the mold face the film has to leave clean. Suregiant’s release film entered mass production for 2.5D advanced packaging in 2024, was applied to panel-level fan-out in 2025, and is advancing to 3D packaging in 2026. A 2.5D compression is wide and relatively flat. Fan-out on a panel moves more resin across a larger area. A 3D stack adds height and more interfaces that can trap residue. Residue that would pass a lab peel test can still stop an automated visual check or contaminate the next shot. Suregiant says it is a qualified supplier to the world’s top five semiconductor manufacturers, with film already in mass production at first-tier advanced packaging. Order visibility runs 2 to 3 years, and customer forecasts reach 5 to 6 years, so the coating line is booked against a package roadmap, not a spot order.

Plant 1 is at full load. Taoyuan Plant 2 completed trial production and is expected to begin official production in December, at 2.5 to 3 times the scale of Plant 1, with a full year of contribution in 2027. Against that, the first three quarters of 2026 produced NT$333 million of revenue, about $10.1 million, NT$229 million of gross profit, NT$175 million of operating profit, NT$140 million of after-tax profit and earnings per share of NT$6.35. Third-quarter revenue was NT$159 million, up 80.76 percent quarter on quarter, and quarterly after-tax profit was NT$66.51 million, up 92.72 percent. Multiplying Plant 1 by 2.5 to 3 does not by itself multiply profit; Yang is counting on a rising share of high-margin advanced-packaging film inside that volume.

That coating film ceases to be the consumable that gates output when the critical step is no longer demolding a compressed package. Grinding tape, supplied to the world’s top ten packaging plants for more than 12 years, is the second product, and a thick single-adhesive-layer version went to first-tier verification in the fourth quarter of 2026 for taller bumps and thinner wafers. The third is hydrolyzable tape, meant to replace temporary bonding adhesives that need laser or ultraviolet debond, using a plant’s existing pure-water clean and skipping the chemical clean. Official samples are expected in mid-2027, with a gradual ramp in 2028. When the line is releasing a thinned, bonded wafer in pure water rather than peeling resin off a compression mold, the extrusion-versus-coating contest on release film no longer decides who can ship. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/e6469aad-1f4f-44de-b766-7be0b0a31a21)

### On the Horizon
- Mid-December 2026: Suregiant’s transfer to the OTC market is expected, at a tentative public-offering price of NT$438 per share.
- 2027: ASEAN agreed with China’s proposal to designate 2027 as the Year of ASEAN-China AI Cooperation, with talks on practical projects still at an early stage.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **Twelve million TPP now needs a US licence if a data centre serves China.**

**What You Need to Know:** Twelve million TPP now needs a US licence if a data centre serves China. The Bureau of Industry and Security interim final rule sets that cap at roughly 750 H100s or about 330 B200s, and it also licences advanced-chip shipments into Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. Centres already serving the covered customers have 90 days to get a licence.

### Top Story
The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule requiring a licence to ship advanced accelerators to any data centre worldwide that provides more than 12 million aggregate TPP to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5, which includes China, TechPowerUp reported. TPP is a chip’s peak dense throughput multiplied by the bit length of the operation; an H100 rates about 15,800 TPP, so the cap is roughly 750 H100s or around 330 B200s, and it also covers linked data centres and indirect access such as a cloud reseller. Fortune and Silicon UK report that a licence is now required to export, re-export or transfer advanced semiconductors to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, which the rule treats as a higher-than-normal diversion risk. Data centres already serving the covered customers have 90 days to obtain a licence. Only commercial recommender systems are exempt; anything that generates text, images, video or code does not qualify. BIS said the rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/354927/u-s-cracks-down-on-china-renting-ai-gpus-through-overseas-data-centers)

### Silicon
**Nvidia Rubin HPC GPU Unveiled at SC26 With 50,000+ CUDA Cores: Tech Times**
Nvidia announced Rubin HPC on Monday at the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago: a Vera Rubin-family GPU with more than 50,000 CUDA cores, hardware for sparse-data acceleration and seventh-generation NVLink, due in 2028. AI Weekly reports that the current Rubin tops out at 28,672 CUDA cores, and that NVLink 7 keeps the 3.6 terabytes per second of per-GPU bandwidth already shipping on NVLink 6. Nvidia named four patterns the sparse hardware is meant to speed up: sparse matrix operations, stencil computations, sorting and reductions. The same conference material describes a Vera CPU rack of 192 CPUs, about 300 terabytes of memory and 1 petabyte of storage, arriving in early 2027. Tech Times calculates that on the June 2026 TOP500 list El Capitan posted 1.809 exaflops on LINPACK and 17.41 petaflops on HPCG, about 1 percent of LINPACK speed, the memory-bound gap this part is aimed at. Source: [techtimes.com](https://www.techtimes.com/articles/330881/20261117/nvidia-rubin-hpc-gpu-unveiled-sc26-50000-cuda-cores-no-memory-bandwidth-figure.htm) · [aiweekly.co](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/nvidia-teases-rubin-hpc-gpu-50000-cuda-cores-ships-2028)

**MLPerf Training v6.1 Adds Post-Training Test: Tech Times**
MLCommons on Monday published MLPerf Training v6.1, adding the first post-training benchmark and the first results from Nvidia’s Rubin-generation GPUs and Google’s Ironwood TPU. Twenty-four organizations submitted 153 systems that produced 250 results; 57 of those systems, 37 percent, ran in the cloud, up from 29 percent in v6.0 six months ago, twelve used 1,000 or more accelerators, and the largest used 10,240. On the new Qwen3.5-397B reinforcement-learning test, Nvidia reports 10.44 minutes on Vera Rubin NVL72 at 1,024 GPUs, Google Cloud reports 18.02 minutes on 640 Ironwood TPUs that reached 0.765 accuracy against a 0.69 target, and CoreWeave reports 22.78 minutes on 256 GB200 GPUs across four racks, with 128 GPUs on training and 128 on generation. Those runs differ in chip generation, chip count and how the work was split, so Tech Times says they show what each system did rather than which chip is faster. On DeepSeek-V3 at 1,024 GPUs, Nvidia reports 4.14 minutes for Rubin and 8.03 minutes for GB300; a 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 cluster across 160 racks set the round’s fastest absolute time at 1.38 minutes. Nvidia claims up to 2x per-GPU versus an optimized GB300 NVL72 baseline, and CoreWeave reports 17.65 minutes for DeepSeek-V3 on 256 Rubin GPUs against 48.40 minutes on its own GB200 at the same count, a comparison it says MLCommons has not verified. Source: [techtimes.com](https://www.techtimes.com/articles/330890/20261117/mlperf-training-v61-adds-post-training-test-nvidia-google-coreweave-results-not-comparable.htm)

**Samsung is developing custom HBM4E memory for Meta's AI chips on a 2nm base die: MLQ.ai**
MLQ.ai reports that a Korean outlet says Samsung is developing custom HBM4E for Meta’s AI chips on a 2nm base die. The report describes development, not a shipped part. Source: [mlq.ai](https://mlq.ai/news/samsung-is-developing-custom-hbm4e-memory-for-metas-ai-chips-on-a-2nm-base-die-korean-outlet-reports/)

**AMD Says MI455X Delivers 30% Higher Token Throughput Than Nvidia: THE ELEC**
THE ELEC reports that AMD says the MI455X delivers 30 percent higher token throughput than Nvidia. iTWire frames the same claim as a 30 percent inference lead over Nvidia’s Vera Rubin, and says the MI450X widens the Instinct MI400 series. Source: [thelec.net](https://www.thelec.net/news/articleView.html?idxno=15660) · [itwire.com](https://itwire.com/business-it-news/data/spectacular-strategic-supremely-timed-amd-s-mi-series-delivers-widened-instinct-mi400-with-the-mi450x-as-mi455x-claims-a-30-inference-lead-over-nvidias-vera-rubin)

### Data Centres & Power
**HPE-Built Lux AI Cluster Debuts at No. 14 on the TOP500: HPCwire**
At SC26, HPE announced that Lux, an AI cluster it developed with AMD for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, debuted at number 14 on the TOP500. HPE says Lux is the first AI system to support the US Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/hpe-built-lux-ai-cluster-debuts-at-no-14-on-the-top500/)

**Vertiv Opens ATLAS Lab to Test AI Power and Cooling Infrastructure: HPCwire**
Vertiv opened the ATLAS lab in Columbus, Ohio, on November 17 to prove power, thermal-management and controls infrastructure for AI factories before next-generation compute reaches the market. The lab is built for system-level testing of density, speed, scale, complexity and dynamic load profiles. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/vertiv-opens-atlas-lab-to-test-ai-power-and-cooling-infrastructure/)

**UC Berkeley and Berkeley Lab Join Schmidt Science Computing Network: HPCwire**
The University of California, Berkeley and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory will join the Schmidt Science Computing Network, a distributed network meant to expand advanced computing available for science, HPCwire reported. The move was announced November 16. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/uc-berkeley-and-berkeley-lab-join-schmidt-science-computing-network/)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**Singapore's Megaspeed under criminal investigation over Nvidia chip exports, US confirms: TRT World**
The US Departments of Commerce and Justice confirmed on Monday that they are conducting a criminal investigation into Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed over suspected semiconductor export-control violations. Commerce launched the inquiry in 2024 after detecting suspicious chip-diversion activity, requested Nvidia’s sales records in May 2025, and Nvidia placed Megaspeed on an internal no-sell list the following month. Bureau of Industry and Security agents then inspected Megaspeed sites in Singapore with local law enforcement and interviewed then-executive Alice Huang; the Justice Department subsequently took the lead. The agencies said authorities under the Trump administration have charged 17 defendants in six cases involving billions of dollars worth of semiconductors, and that monetary penalties for export-control violations had increased 18-fold compared with the previous administration. Fortune, citing a November 16 Straits Times report, says Indonesian officials who inspected PT Megaspeed International Indonesia found unused server racks with missing GPUs. Source: [trtworld.com](https://www.trtworld.com/article/9cd5943c59cb) · [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/354921/u-s-departments-of-commerce-and-justice-issue-rare-joint-statement-on-the-nvidia-megaspeed-investigation) · [fortune.com](https://fortune.com/2026/11/17/sg-us-ai-chip-controls-southeast-asia/)

**Singapore defends status as a trusted business hub after the U.S. rolls out new AI chip controls: Fortune**
A Singapore government spokesperson said on November 16 that Singapore does not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent other countries’ laws, and that the government is engaging US authorities and affected companies on the new measure. Thailand’s vice minister for commerce, Kirida Bhaopichitr, told CNBC the country is prepared, does not want to be a transshipment hub from the US to China, and will scrutinize data centres more closely. Indonesia said it is reviewing the rule and seeking industry input on data-centre operations and investment. TRT World reports that Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the move economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, and said Beijing would take necessary measures. Malaysia’s Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry said on November 13 it is checking with customs whether chips brought into Malaysia were re-exported in accordance with the law. Digital Realty’s Serene Nah said the measure is still an interim rule and licence details are not out yet; the company operates three facilities in Singapore and, in June, opened a Cyberjaya campus designed for approximately 32 megawatts. Source: [fortune.com](https://fortune.com/2026/11/17/sg-us-ai-chip-controls-southeast-asia/) · [trtworld.com](https://www.trtworld.com/article/eb0cee8982d2)

**NVIDIA Board of Directors Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee: NVIDIA Newsroom**
Nvidia’s board has established a standing National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to oversee national-security policy, export-control compliance and global trade risk. Director Suzanne Nora Johnson will chair it, with directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members; it will meet at least quarterly and retain independent outside experts. The company’s National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report to the committee and to interim CEO Colette Kress on day-to-day operations. Source: [nvidianews.nvidia.com](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-board-of-directors-establishes-national-security-and-export-control-oversight-committee)

**TSMC puts construction safety ahead of capacity milestones in its 2026 supplier awards: digitimes**
At its 2026 Supply Chain Management Forum in Hsinchu on November 17, TSMC said this year’s supplier awards gave more weight to construction safety, sustainability, global support and localization. Digitimes reports that shift as a change in how the company judges suppliers, ahead of capacity milestones. Source: [digitimes.com](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20261117VL219/tsmc-2026-capacity-fab-supply.html)

### Also Today
**Intel Says D270 GPU Delivers Up to 5.9x Nvidia's Throughput: THE ELEC**
THE ELEC reports that Intel says its D270 GPU delivers up to 5.9 times Nvidia’s throughput. Source: [thelec.net](https://www.thelec.net/news/articleView.html?idxno=15700)

**A supercomputing lab on any desk: Nvidia unveils DGX Spark HPC Dev Kit with 512 GB of memory: Notebookcheck**
Nvidia has unveiled a DGX Spark HPC Dev Kit with 512 gigabytes of memory, a step up from the 64-gigabyte and 128-gigabyte Spark configurations already on the market. Source: [notebookcheck.net](https://www.notebookcheck.net/A-supercomputing-lab-on-any-desk-Nvidia-unveils-DGX-Spark-HPC-Dev-Kit-with-512-GB-of-memory.1452326.0.html)

**Chip Industry Technical Paper Roundup: Nov. 17: Semiconductor Engineering**
Semiconductor Engineering’s November 17 paper roundup includes hardware-based location checks for AI-chip smuggling, HBM4 controller partitioning, and embedded ECC for AI weight protection. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-technical-paper-roundup-nov-17/)

### The Teardown: A Million Dollars a Megawatt in the Tank
Immersion cooling removes heat by putting the server in a dielectric liquid instead of blowing air across a heatsink. The fluid touches the board, so the thermal path is component to liquid to a heat exchanger, not component to air to a coil. In single-phase immersion the liquid stays liquid; pumps move it, and a heat exchanger dumps the heat elsewhere. Because the bath does the cooling, the hall no longer has to be designed around airflow, and the method uses no water for evaporative cooling. Data Center Knowledge notes that this also cuts some operational risk by removing fans and airflow dependencies, and that the technique has existed for decades. As of 2026 it is still not how major operators cool production halls. Headlines have been pilots, demonstrations and proofs of concept, including Microsoft’s experiment earlier this decade. Direct-to-chip liquid, which runs coolant in pipes beside the processor and leaves the server in a conventional rack, is the liquid method projected to grow.

The money is why the tank loses the bid. Data Center Knowledge cites a study putting immersion at about $1 million per megawatt of IT load, against $650,000 per megawatt for direct-to-chip. That is $350,000 more capital for every megawatt before a watt of IT is turned on. Operators trying to energize capacity quickly feel that gap on day one. The operating side looks better, and the article gives a worked cluster rather than a slogan. Adam Silva Consulting estimates that cooling a 64-rack AI cluster over 10 years costs $42 million with advanced air, $31 million with direct-to-chip liquid, and $28 million with single-phase immersion. Air to immersion is a $14 million difference across that decade. Direct-to-chip to immersion is a $3 million difference. The tank wins the 10-year cooling bill, and it wins by less against the liquid method operators can adopt without throwing out the rack. A $350,000-per-megawatt premium has to be earned back from that $3 million gap, plus whatever footprint and energy the bath saves. The article does not convert the 64 racks into megawatts, so the payback cannot be stated as a number of years; the comparison that is in the source is already enough to see the problem. Three million dollars of operating advantage against a capital premium measured per megawatt is a hard sell when the alternative keeps the cabinet, the lift, and the technician’s existing procedure.

The rest of the hesitation is how the building is run. Airflow stops being the constraint that sets row pitch and white-space layout, so the architecture can change, and the article argues it should. Servers come out of a tank, not a cabinet. Monitoring, service workflows and technician training all move with that. Direct-to-chip also changes design, but it preserves more of the server-and-rack habit, which is why incremental adoption is easier. The point at which the $1 million-per-megawatt tank stops losing to the $650,000 direct-to-chip install is the point at which heat density and water limits make a $3 million, 10-year edge on a 64-rack cluster, and a $14 million edge against advanced air, worth redrawing the hall and retraining the floor. Data Center Knowledge’s condition is concrete: if power-hungry training and inference keep expanding, and if pressure to cut water and energy rises with them, the bath gets more attractive. If that boom flattens before operators make the capital and the cultural commit, immersion stays where it is in 2026, a pilot beside a production hall still built for racks. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/cooling/why-immersion-cooling-still-hasn-t-gone-mainstream)

### On the Horizon
- Data centres already serving covered customers have 90 days from the interim final rule to obtain a licence.
- Nvidia’s Vera CPU rack, 192 CPUs with about 300 terabytes of memory, is described as arriving in early 2027.
- Rubin HPC, with more than 50,000 CUDA cores, is due in 2028.
